title: Psychiatric manifestations in dengue: A case series and review
case_text:
Case 1: A 32-year adult man working as a daily wage laborer was admitted to the general medicine ward with history of high-grade fever with chills and rigors, not sleeping and not eating for 3 days. The patient loose stools, and generalized body aches since the day of admission. After hospitalization, medical examinations were conducted. The test results showed a positive IgM ELISA for dengue. Further tests indicated a platelet count of 32000/mul; total leukocyte count of 6300/cm with lymphocytes at 52%. The patient was diagnosed with dengue fever accompanied by thrombocytopenia. On 2nd day of admission, a psychiatry referral was given for sudden episodes of irritability and altered behavior. He was overtalkative, overfamiliar, irritable, and had overgrooming behavior and big talks. The patient did not have a history of psychiatric illness, nor did he have any family history of psychiatric illness. MRI of the brain was normal. MSE revealed authoritative behavior with increased motor activity of the patient, increased rate, tone volume of speech with decreased reaction time of speech and ideas of grandiosity. The patient was diagnosed with Secondary mood syndrome with manic symptoms according to ICD 11 considering no prior predisposition to psychiatric illness and direct temporal relation of onset of his psychiatric symptoms to dengue fever. The patient was started on Tab. Divalproate 250 mg and gradually increased to 500mg. He showed improvement within 8 days and complete remission of symptoms in 14 days.
Case 2: A 21-year young man studying BTech was admitted in the general medicine ward with the history of high-grade fever of 3 days duration. Patient had fever, loose stools, vomiting and generalized body ache 2 days. Investigations were done on the 2nd day of fever. His dengue IgM ELISA test resulted in a positive result; other tests showed a platelet count of 24,000/mul, a total leukocyte counts of 7,400/cmm, and 48% lymphocytes. He was diagnosed to have thrombocytopenia and dengue fever. A psychiatry referral was given for sudden episodes of irritability and altered behavior. During interview, he was over talkativeness, restless, and authoritative. He was feeling that his friends are jealous of him and are trying to kill him and reported decreased need for sleep. There was no past or family history of psychiatric disorders. MRI of the brain was normal. MSE revealed authoritative behavior with increased motor activity of the patient, increased rate tone volume of speech with decreased reaction time, grandiose ideas, and delusion of persecution. He was diagnosed to have Secondary mood syndrome with manic symptoms according to ICD 11. He was treated with Tab Risperidone 4 mg and Tab. Trihexyphenidyl 2mg and showed resolution of symptoms within 10 days.
A 37-year adult woman homemaker by profession was admitted to the general medicine ward with the complaints of joints pain, high grade fever, gum bleeding, petechiae, nose bleed and loose stools for 2 days. On the third day of the fever, investigations were conducted. Her dengue IgM ELISA result was positive; other investigations revealed a platelet count of 12000/mul, total leukocyte count: 4700/cmm with lymphocytes 46%. She was found to have thrombocytopenia and dengue hemorrhagic fever. The MRI brain revealed no abnormality. A psychiatry referral was given after 10 days of admission for persistent pervasive low mood, decreased confidence and self-esteem, passive death wishes and suicidal ideations, frequent episodes of apprehension and palpitations and disturbed sleep and appetite for 8 days. On interview, she reported feeling of sadness without any reason. She would feel persistently sad and apprehensive even though she is not worried about her medical condition. The patient did not have a past or family history of psychiatric disorders. MSE revealed oriented patient with anxious mood, reactive distressed affect, worrying thoughts with intact insight and judgement. She was diagnosed with Secondary mood syndrome with depressive symptoms according to ICD 11. She was treated with Tab Sertraline 50 mg and Tab clonazepam 0.25mg and showed improvement within 17 days.
Case 4: A 56-year adult woman, a school teacher by profession, was admitted to the general medicine ward with complaints of joints pain, high grade fever for 2 days. Investigations were done on the 3rd day of fever. Her IgM ELISA for dengue was positive; platelet count of 32000/mul, total leukocyte count: 8300/cc with lymphocytes 48%. She was diagnosed as a case of dengue fever with thrombocytopenia. MRI revealed no abnormalities. A psychiatry referral was given after 3 days of admission for altered behavior. On interviewing, patient had irritability, disturbed sleep, and appetite, decreased interaction with family, suspicious of her family members and fearfulness. Patient had no prior history of psychiatric illness and no family history of psychiatric illness as well. MSE revealed oriented patient with fearful mood, reactive distressed affect with delusion of persecution and reference with poor insight and impaired judgment. The diagnosis of Secondary psychotic syndrome with delusions was made according to ICD 11. She was treated with Tab Risperidone 3 mg and showed improvement in 11 days.

You are an expert clinician–educator in tropical and infectious diseases.
Your job is to transform a published clinical case report into a standardized admission diagnostic teaching case following the Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology.

In terms of style, model your output on NEJM’s Clinicopathologic Conferences ("Case Records of the Massachusetts General Hospital").

RULES (Read Carefully — No Exceptions):
1. SOURCE FIDELITY:
   - Extract facts ONLY from the supplied case report.
   - Do NOT invent, embellish, or smooth out missing clinical data.
   - Never extrapolate findings not explicitly mentioned.

2. THE ADMISSION BREAKPOINT PRINCIPLE (CRITICAL):
   - The <case_prompt> represents what an emergency triage clinician knows on Day 1 BEFORE confirmatory tests return.
   - INCLUDE in <case_prompt>: Demographics, travel/occupational/vector exposures (freshwater contact, insect bites, animal exposure), symptom chronology, vital signs, physical exam findings, and initial triage laboratory/imaging results (CBC, platelets, basic metabolic panel, LFTs, urinalysis, plain chest radiograph, bedside ultrasound).
   - STRICTLY EXCLUDE from <case_prompt>:
     * Any mention of the disease name or pathogen genus/species (e.g., do not write "Leptospirosis", "Burkholderia", "Leishmania", "Paragonimus").
     * Confirmatory send-out PCR panels, serological titers, blood culture organism identifications, or biopsy histopathology.
     * The clinical outcome or treatment response (these belong in the diagnostic reasoning, not the presentation).

3. STRUCTURE OF <diagnostic_reasoning>:
   - Enumerate all alternative candidate diagnoses considered in the text.
   - For each candidate, provide a concise summary explaining why it was considered and why it was ruled out in this patient, followed by a direct verbatim quote from the article in quotation marks.
   - Conclude with the Diagnostic Pivot: the pivotal clinical and confirmatory turning point that established the confirmed diagnosis.

4. TARGET CANONICAL DISEASE:
   - The verified ground-truth disease for this patient is: Dengue
   - Disease subtype / specific manifestation: psychiatric manifestations of dengue infection
